prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is the strongest candidate on the table on chemical originality and breadth of support: it was ranked in the top three by six of eight members, which is more than any other candidate. The central idea, that a small molecule can bring an E3 ligase and a target together so that the target is ubiquitylated and removed catalytically, replaces occupancy-driven pharmacology with event-driven pharmacology. That is a new chemical principle, not just a new tool. The mechanism has been reproduced in many independent laboratories, structure-guided design (VHL ligands, ternary-complex cooperativity) has made degraders drug-like, and many clinical-stage compounds exist. Crews and Deshaies supply the founding concept and early demonstrations, and Ciulli supplies the structure-guided chemistry that turned the concept into a design discipline. That gives a coherent three-person story with one achievement.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC has been approved, so clinical impact is promised rather than demonstrated, and the prize would be awarded on mechanistic and conceptual grounds with the main clinical test still pending. The attribution is also strained. The thalidomide-cereblon molecular-glue strand (Handa, Ito and others) is a distinct line of discovery, and a three-name limit forces us either to omit it or to define the citation narrowly around heterobifunctional degraders. Two colleagues (Brzezinski and Chabes) put Handa in their trio and several others flag him as a necessary omission, and I cannot dismiss that. If the committee judges that PROTACs and glues cannot be separated, the case is weaker than the raw ranking count suggests.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks perovskites first for their very clear first demonstration, rapid independent reproduction and rising efficiency, and uses Handa in place of Ciulli in his degradation trio because Handa and Ito identified cereblon as the thalidomide target.
responses.response: I take the cereblon argument seriously, and it is the best objection to my own trio. The thalidomide mechanism is the only part of this field that is already attached to approved drugs, so omitting it is a real cost. But I still prefer Ciulli to Handa for a prize built on the PROTAC concept: the citation then describes one coherent invention, with a founding concept (Crews, Deshaies) and a design chemistry (Ciulli). A Handa slot would shift the prize toward molecular glues, where credit spreads across Ito, Handa, Gray and others and a clean three-person split does not exist. On perovskites I agree with the scientific merit but remain unsure about maturity. Stability, lead toxicity and commercial scale-up are open, and the credit among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis is at least as contested as in degradation, so I do not see perovskites as the safer choice.

responses.point: Chabes ranks massively parallel sequencing first because reversible-terminator chemistry rests on engineered nucleotide analogues and polymerase behaviour, and proposes Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Rothberg.
responses.response: I agree with the chemistry and with the maturity: this is the one candidate where recognition is overdue and not early, and I ranked it second myself. My reservation is about Rothberg. His pyrosequencing and semiconductor platforms are a parallel technological route and not the Solexa chemistry, so adding him mixes two routes and leaves Mayer, Ju and the pyrosequencing precursors as arbitrary exclusions. I would keep the two-person core, Balasubramanian and Klenerman. The remaining question is whether a committee that wants a chemistry prize is comfortable that much of the impact came through instrument engineering and industrial scale-up. I think so, but the citation must stay anchored to the nucleotide chemistry and single-molecule detection, not to genomics generally.

responses.point: Sparr ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first, arguing that pH-dependent charge and non-bilayer lipid phase behaviour make RNA delivery possible, that the field is clinically proven at global scale, and that the 2023 Medicine prize covered nucleoside modification and not the carrier.
responses.response: I find the physical-chemistry argument persuasive, and the point that the 2023 prize left the carrier unrecognized is a fair one. My difficulty is attribution. Cullis, Hope, Madden and MacLachlan built the ionizable-lipid formulation, Anderson and Langer built lipidoid libraries, and a great deal of the decisive optimization happened inside companies. A three-name limit forces choices that I think the record does not clearly support, and two of your own ranking colleagues propose different trios. I would also be wary of how close this sits to the mRNA vaccine prize in Medicine in 2023. If we can agree on a clean citation and on names, I would put it at about the same level as sequencing, but I do not see that agreement yet.

responses.point: Somfai ranks C-N cross-coupling first as a synthetic-efficiency achievement with clean two-person attribution (Buchwald and Hartwig), and ranks degradation last of his three listed candidates because no PROTAC has been approved.
responses.response: The attribution for C-N coupling is cleaner than for any other candidate here, and I accept that maturity is not an issue. My doubt is about novelty relative to the 2010 cross-coupling prize: this is a major extension of a recognized reaction family and not a new principle, and the committee has historically been reluctant to return to an area it has recently covered. On your maturity objection to degradation, I partly agree and have said so in my case against. But the mechanism and its reproducibility are not in doubt, and what is missing is regulatory approval, not scientific confirmation. I would rather accept the modest timing risk for a genuinely new mode of action than reward a very good extension of known chemistry.

uncertainties: Whether the citation should cover PROTACs only or include molecular glues (Handa, Ito), and whether a three-name limit makes that choice unavoidable.
Whether the absence of an approved PROTAC drug is a decisive timing objection or only a minor one.
Whether the two-person core Balasubramanian and Klenerman is defensible if colleagues insist on including Rothberg.
Whether a two-part prize combining degradation with another achievement is useful, given that the three-person limit would leave each part with only one or two names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the candidates on the shortlist. I work in nanophysics, thermoelectrics and molecular motors, none of which overlaps with the shortlisted laureates. As chair I will keep my own role neutral and try to elicit disagreement, not manage it away.
